title: Learn Docker
summary: Containers package a program with everything it needs. Learn to run them, serve a website from one, and clean up after yourself.

lessons.title: Hello, containers
lessons.story: Docker runs programs in containers: little isolated boxes made from images. Let's check Docker is here and run the classic first container.

steps.task: Check that Docker is installed: docker --version
hints: Type docker --version in the Terminal.
steps.explain: The docker command is the client. It talks to the Docker daemon, a background service that does the work.

steps.task: Run your first container: docker run hello-world
hints: Type docker run hello-world. The first time, Docker downloads the image.
steps.explain: Docker didn't have the image, so it pulled it from Docker Hub, created a container from it, and ran it.

steps.task: See every container, including finished ones: docker ps -a
hints: Plain docker ps only shows running containers. -a means all.
Type docker ps -a
steps.explain: The container printed its message and exited, so its STATUS is Exited (0). It still exists until you remove it.

lessons.title: Images
lessons.story: An image is a read-only template: a small Linux system plus a program. Containers are running copies of images.

steps.task: Download the tiny Alpine Linux image: docker pull alpine
hints: Type docker pull alpine
steps.explain: pull downloads an image without running it. Alpine is a whole Linux distribution in under 8 MB.

steps.task: List the images you have: docker images
hints: Type docker images
steps.explain: Each image has a repository name, a tag (latest is the default) and an ID.

steps.task: Run one command inside an Alpine container to see which Linux it is: docker run alpine cat /etc/os-release
hints: Anything after the image name is the command to run inside the container.
Type docker run alpine cat /etc/os-release
steps.explain: Your system isn't Alpine, but the container is: it brings its own files. That's what makes containers portable.

lessons.title: Serving a website
lessons.story: Containers are great for services that keep running, like web servers. You'll run nginx in the background and visit it.

steps.task: Start nginx in the background, named web, with port 8080 on this computer going to port 80 in the container: docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx
hints: -d runs it in the background (detached). --name gives it a name. -p HOST:CONTAINER publishes a port.
Type docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx
steps.explain: Docker printed the new container's full ID. The container keeps running after the command returns.

hints: Type docker ps and look at the STATUS and PORTS columns.
steps.explain: PORTS shows 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp: requests to port 8080 here reach port 80 inside the container.

steps.task: Visit the website from the terminal: curl localhost:8080
hints: curl fetches a web page and prints it.
Type curl localhost:8080
steps.explain: That HTML came from nginx inside the container, through the port you published.

steps.task: See what the server recorded: docker logs web
hints: Type docker logs web
steps.explain: Containers write logs to their output, and docker logs shows them: here, your curl request.

lessons.title: Stopping and cleaning up
lessons.story: Containers and images take up space until you remove them. Let's practise the clean-up routine on a container of your own.

steps.task: Start a container to practise on: docker run -d --name scratch nginx
hints: Type docker run -d --name scratch nginx
steps.explain: Naming containers makes them easy to refer to. Otherwise Docker invents a name like jolly_turing.

steps.task: Try to remove it while it's still running: docker rm scratch
hints: This is meant to fail. Type docker rm scratch and read the error.
steps.explain: Docker protects running containers. Stop them first, or force it with docker rm -f.

hints: Type docker stop scratch
steps.explain: stop asks the program to shut down cleanly. The container still exists, just not running.

steps.task: Now remove it: docker rm scratch
hints: Type docker rm scratch, then docker ps -a to check it's gone.
steps.explain: Removed for good. docker run --rm removes a container automatically when it exits.

lessons.title: Configuring with environment variables
lessons.story: Many images are configured with environment variables. A database is a good example: it won't start without a password.

steps.task: Try to start the PostgreSQL database without any settings: docker run postgres
hints: This is meant to fail. Type docker run postgres and read why.
steps.explain: The image refused to start: it needs a password for the database's superuser.

steps.task: Start it in the background named db with a password: docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres
hints: -e NAME=value sets an environment variable inside the container.
Type docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres
steps.explain: Configuration that changes between environments (passwords, URLs) goes in variables, not in the image.

steps.task: Look inside the running container's environment: docker exec db env
hints: docker exec runs a command inside a running container.
Type docker exec db env
steps.explain: exec is how you get into a running container to look around or debug.
